reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The manuscript by Murakawa et al focuses on domain movements during copper amine oxidase catalysis.
Mix-and-inject serial crystallography, an advanced technique to capture time-resolved protein structures in real time provides
structural insight into enzyme catalysis accompanying the active-site conformational changes that are unobservable by
studies in solution.
This study is very interesting not only to fellow specialists working in related areas but also to the general readership of
Nature Commun., attracting attention, and therefore is recommended for publication in this journal.
However, the followings can be considered before the publication.
In Fig.3a, is the position where Phenylethylamine(2-PEA) enters during the reaction from TPQpsb to TPQamr between
TPQamr and TPQsq?
In Fig.2 and Fig.3, the observed difference of 3mS from 22mS to 25mS seems to be larger than others. Are there any reason
of that in the measurement?
In Fig.3, how do you measure the average occupancy of TPQamr and TPQsq? Is the way different form that used in Fig.4?
Lines 142-143
"The orders of the observed rates of these steps (TPQpsb → TPQamr [50–100 ms] and TPQamr → TPQsq [100–1000 ms])
were compatible with the rate constants (102 and 39 s−1, respectively) determined in solution at 4°C and pH 6.8 via
stopped-flow measurements23 but slower by 10–50 fold."
Is the expression of "orders ---- were compatible with the rate constants" correct?
Lines 239-241
"Collectively, these results suggest that the gradual transition from TPQamr to TPQsq during 100–1000 ms (Fig. 3c) is due to
the slow replacement of PAA by 2-PEA depending on the diffusion-controlled rates of desorption of PAA from the substrate-
binding pocket and re-binding of 2-PEA."
At "Line 87", "under anaerobic conditions at pH 9.0 so that the pH-dependent equilibrium between TPQamr and TPQsq
shifts toward TPQsq24" is written, while the gradual transition from TPQamr to TPQsq during 100–1000 ms is due to the
slow replacement of PAA by 2-PEA.
At least in crystals, this equilibrium reaction does not occur depending on pH?
In Extended Fig.2, only data of 0 ms was measured in solutions without 2-PEA.
Is it not appropriate to compare with the data from 22 minutes onwards?
In Extended Fig.2, actually, the length of a-axis in data of 0 ms is different from each of those of (L) and (S).
It is better to show data of 0mS and that of 22mS-1000mS, respectively.
"Method section" (Line 356-424" is described between "References section": (Lines 263-354) and (Lines 426-460).
Is it OK?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Review Manuscript “Real time capture of domain movements during copper amine oxidase catalysis by mix-and-inject serial
crystallography”
The authors Murakawa and collaborators present a very comprehensive time -resolved serial crystallography study on a
copper amine oxidase with time point ranging from 22 ms to 1 s. This work follows the reaction cycle of AGAO mixed with 2-
PEA in anaerobic conditions using the sample delivery method MISC (mix-and-inject serial crystallography). All the
experimental details (apart from the stop flow experiments) are provided either in the methods or the supplementary
information. We have only minor remarks on this paper, and we strongly support the publication in Nature Communications.
SI
• Additional information on the pH/ pKa and rates of the reactions in solution in the scheme in Extended Data Fig. 1 would
be helpful.
• Additionally, the stopped flow data that has been used to calculate these rates and is referred to several times in the text
should really be in the SI, and the details should be in the methods. Or if this is already published data then it needs a
reference.
• Could you add a figure giving the the chemical structures of PAA and 2-PEA
• Extended figure 5 & 6: 2-PEA diffusion in solvent channel: there is a program that allows the user to visualize the solvent
channel: MAP_CHANNELS by Juers and Ruffin (J. Appl. Cryst 2014). This program or maybe a newer program could help
to measure the solvent channel, and it could help to support or explain why 2D diffusion model is preferred.
Manuscript
• Abstract
o Line 38-39: "active-site conformational changes that are unobservable by studies in solution" is quite a broad statement
and may not be true, maybe NMR in solution could help. Could you please comment.
• Results / MISC measurement and data processing section
o Line 86: A reference is missing for "(2-PEA; the most preferred substrate)"
• Discussion section:
o Since there are 2 different redox states of Cu between TPQamr and TPQsp, could X-ray Emission Spectroscopy help to
corroborate some hypothesis about the slow replacement of PAA by 2-PEA? If you had access to this technique, would you
use it, and would it help?
o The temperature differences between the stopped flow experiments (15 C) and MISC experiments (26 C) could also be a
reason for differences in the rates.
Methods
• We would like a bit more details on the sample consumption. On average how many ml / ul (or mg of protein) have been
used for each time point?
• The MISC sample delivery method has been used quite extensively in the US with Schmidt and collaborators. We were not
aware that SACLA is offering this sample delivery method. Could you please give more details on MISC: is it provided by the
facility? Or by collaboration? Is it the same nozzle design used by Schmidt et al?
Additional comments from the team review
Line 28 (within the abstract)
Please state somewhere that the time-revolved studies are for the reductive half reaction.
Line 32:
Please state the average crystal size used for the tr-SFX work
(see line 84 for values; 2.5 × 4 μm parallelogram plate × < 1 μm thick).
Line 33: “amine substrate”
ambiguous, please state what substrate was used for this study (2-phenylethylamine).
Line 54
a microcrystal suspension of an enzyme is mixed with the substrate and ejected to the XFEL emission point,
“emission” should probably be “interaction”
Lines 56 – 57
Namely, MISC is a crystallographic version of a classical continuous-flow or stopped-flow technique used for detection of
time-resolved reaction intermediates formed during enzyme catalysis in solution15,16.
Reads better as:
Namely, MISC is a crystallographic version of a classical transient kinetic, spectroscopic analysis of continuous-flow or
stopped-flow technique used for detection of time-resolved reaction intermediates formed during enzyme catalysis in
solution15,16.
Line 86 “(2-PEA; the most preferred substrate)”
Please provide KM, and kcat values for relevant pH values here and provide appropriate references.
Line 96: “we noted unusual distributions of”
As you state a few lines later, this is fit to a simple bimodal distribution; therefore, please replace “unusual” with “bimodal”.
Line 101 and following sentences: “indicating the presence of two microcrystal regions with unit lattices of different a-axis
lengths...”
This sentence implies two different microdomains within the microcrystals, which may be true and could be consistent with
the partially bleached crystals shown with macrocrystals in Extended Figure 3. However, the bimodal distribution only
demonstrates that successful indexing of the tr-SFX images reveals that there are two, non-isomorphic populations in the
whole slurry. The illustration in Extended Data Fig. 3 suggests that the two species result from X-ray a narrow X-ray beam
passing through the flat face of the crystal plate. The X-ray beam shape is Gaussian, not a top-hat profile, and so there is not
such a big difference between the crystal and X-ray beam sizes. Indeed, the thin plate dimension is smaller than X-ray
beam. Moreover, the X-ray beam passed through randomly oriented crystals; it is possible that indexing may fail if/when the
X-ray beam passes through the bleached and non-bleached regions of the microcrystals. Given that the unit cell changes by
such a small amount (~0.3%), it is likely that indexing probably still succeeds in these cases too.
Analysis of the data from Extended Data Table 1 indicates that the a-axis unit cell edge for all of the timepoint datasets is
different compared to the t = 0, ground state. The % change for the “Long” cell datasets are all small and positive 0.295,
0.348, and 0.191 for the 22, 25, and 50 ms datasets, respectively. However, the % change for the “Short” cell species and all
of the longer timepoints across the series are also all small but negative (-0.124, -0.202, -0.197, -0.191, -0.217, -0.238,
-0.243, -0.321, -0.295). The distribution for first three timpoints are clearly bimodal, but more homogeneous for the later six
timepoint data.
Figure 2 and Extended Data Table 1:
Please annotate the image (or indicate in the legend) the unit cell dimension for the peak of each species. Are these the
same values reported in Extended Data Table 1?
Extended Data Fig. 3
Please comment on why the image of the large macrocrystal indicates that the crystal had not fully reacted even after 30
minutes. The tr-SFX data assumes many thousands of random orientations to sample the whole Ewald sphere and thereby
build up the complete dataset. So, the tr-SFX results with microcrystals indicates that only about 1 second is needed for a
complete reductive half reaction?
Please support the statement, “strict directionality of substrate diffusion” with an analysis and appropriate figure(s) of the
crystal packing and solvent channels with respect to the observable crystal parallelogram plate morphology. If this analysis
has been done in another paper, then it should be referenced. For instance, examination of the lattice packing in PDB code
3WA2 (with different unit cell edge lengths in C121 space group) clearly reveals two ~ orthogonal dimensions with rather
large solvent channels and a third orientation with much smaller channels.
Extended Data Fig. 6
This figure is a good place to show the crystal lattice packing and how it impacts access to the active sites within the lattice.

2022A6705, 2022A8020, 2022B6705, 2022B8013, 2023A6805, 2023A8009, 2023B6805, 2023B8013, 2024A8021, and

which is fine and it is appropriate to indicate which SACLA beamtimes contributed to the publication. However, it is very

Discussion
Time-dependent decrease in the number of diffraction images of 22–50 ms (L) and concomitant
increase in that of 22–50 ms (S) (Fig. 3) reflect the progress of substrate diffusion into the
microcrystals. As shown in Fig. 5, the map calculated by the program MAP_CHANNELSref exhibited
a planar solvent channel that expands to the direction parallel to the b- and c-axes, suggesting that
the amine substrate easily diffuses in the two directions. Moreover, the entrances to the substrate
channel (Extended Data Fig. 6) are connected to this solvent channel (shown by red arrows in Fig.
5). By contrast, the map indicated that the substrate can hardly diffuse in the direction parallel to the
a-axis due to the discontinuous solvent channel interrupted by a layer of enzyme molecules.

crystal thin section is negligible (Extended Data Fig. 5), amine substrate requires approximately 120
ms to diffuse into the entire volume of the microcrystals.

Abstract
Protein dynamics play a crucial role in various physiological functions, including enzyme catalysis.
To explore conformational changes during enzyme catalysis, we conducted mix-and-inject serial
crystallography, an advanced technique to capture time-resolved protein structures in real time,
using the microcrystals of bacterial copper amine oxidase containing a protein-derived quinone
cofactor. Within 50 ms of mixing the microcrystals (< 4 μm) with a preferred substrate (2-
phenylethylamine) under anaerobic conditions (reductive half-reaction), we observed domain
movements associated with substrate binding and formation of a metastable reaction intermediate,
a product Schiff-base of the quinone cofactor. At 100–1000 ms after mixing, conformational
transition from aminoresorcinol to the semiquinone radical forms of the reduced cofactor progressed
gradually, likely depending on the replacement of the product aldehyde by the next-cycle amine
substrate that triggers the cofactor conformational change. Overall, this study provides structural
insight into enzyme catalysis accompanying the active-site conformational changes that are hardly
scrutinized by studies in solution.

We sincerely appreciate your suggestion for additional experiments to reinforce the results of the
MAP_CHANNELS analysis. To address your suggestion under circumstances that a home X-ray
source is unavailable at present, we performed additional synchrotron X-ray diffraction experiments
of the large AGAO crystal to determine the relationship between the crystal lattice orientation and
morphology, using an extra allocated beamtime. Fortunately, the results showed that the a-axis of
the crystal lattice approximately aligns with the shortest dimension (thin section) of the crystal.
Consequently, the b-c plane forms the broad faces of the crystal plate. This structural confirmation
directly supports our conclusion, drawn from the observation of substrate diffusion into the
macrocrystal and also the MAP_CHANNELS analysis, that the substrate amine is poorly permeable
through the broad faces (= across the thin section), being consistent with the proposed two-
dimensional diffusion model. Therefore, we incorporated the new results as supporting evidence
into the Discussion section of the final revised manuscript (as described below), together with
Supplementary Figure 6 (new figure) and a new paragraph in the Methods section.
The a-axis of crystal lattice roughly coincides with the direction of crystal thin section, as confirmed
by an X-ray diffraction analysis of crystal morphology using an AGAO macrocrystal (Supplementary
Fig. 6). Thus, the slow crystal growth along the a-axis may also be explained by the poor contact of
enzyme dimers separated by the solvent channel (Fig. 5).
